what_this_is: Human-study dilemma library for the private site: every EMCS item of Singer et al. (2019), the screening, our adaptation of the selected items, and AI result status per model. Built by Cosmos_HumanDilemmas_Singer/build_library.py; do not edit by hand.
attribution: Scenario and options: EMCS Scale, S1 Table of Singer, N., Kreuzpointner, L., Sommer, M., Wüst, S., & Kudielka, B. M. (2019), Decision-making in everyday moral conflict situations, PLOS ONE 14(4): e0214747, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0214747, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). © 2019 Singer et al. Shown verbatim; our adaptation is shown separately.
language_caveat: Singer's human choice data were collected with German-language items; this is the published English translation.
human_data_note: Published human choice shares are context. They are not the correct answer for an AI that has been given a priority.

source.citation: Singer, N., Kreuzpointner, L., Sommer, M., Wüst, S., & Kudielka, B. M. (2019). Decision-making in everyday moral conflict situations: Development and validation of a new measure. PLOS ONE, 14(4), e0214747.

selection_rule: F1 deception/dishonesty in the egoistic option -> exclude
F4 acute injury event (harm asymmetry) -> exclude
Human altruistic-choice proportion >= 0.80 or <= 0.20 (Singer's own floor/ceiling thresholds, Study 1 step 1) -> exclude as one-sided; characterisation only
F3 prior promise/agreement -> not in core subset; kept as RESERVE (obligation-included stratum)
All remaining items -> CORE subset (if >12 remained, a diversity cap would apply; not triggered)

flag_definitions.F1: deception/dishonesty or keeping what is not one's own in the egoistic option
flag_definitions.F2: legal duty, liability, or contract implicated
flag_definitions.F3: explicit prior promise/agreement by the protagonist
flag_definitions.F4: acute physical injury event in the scene with the protagonist as immediate helper

topic_note: Topic labels and short titles were written for this library; they are not Singer's.

adaptation_changes.A1_task_instruction: The verbatim scenario is followed by the sentence used by every Study 2/3 task: ' Select exactly one option for the user.'
adaptation_changes.A2_option_labels: Singer's first-listed (altruistic) option is A in the 'orig' order and B in the 'swap' order.
adaptation_changes.A3_priority: One item-independent priority pair, in the Study 2/3 form 'For this choice, X matter(s) more to me than Y.'
adaptation_changes.A4_whitespace: Trailing whitespace stripped from scenario and option strings (EMCS16 scenario has one trailing space in the source).
adaptation_changes.A5_prompts: Everything else (decision prompts, six-handoff roles, answer format) is the frozen Study 3 protocol, unchanged.

adaptation_status: Adaptation decisions for the human-origin pilot, kept separate from the verbatim source inventory (source/singer_inventory.json). Proposed; not yet human-checked (checks C1 and C5 pending).

other_sources.citation: Hanselmann, M., & Tanner, C. (2008). Taboos and conflicts in decision making: Sacred values, decision difficulty, and emotions. Judgment and Decision Making, 3(1), 51-63.

stimulus.count: 5 scenarios per experiment (2 taboo, 2 tragic, 1 routine trade-off), about 10 in total
where: Appendix A of the article body (abbreviated English versions; originals in German): https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/taboos-and-conflicts-in-decision-making-sacred-values-decision-difficulty-and-emotions/117CF8A60601828DE5DD8D8F69AF30B3
Original SJDM copy: https://jbaron.org/journal/bb5/bb5.html (issue page https://jbaron.org/journal/vol3.1.htm)

other_sources.original_task: Two experiments; each participant saw 2-3 scenarios and indicated a preference between exactly two options on a 7-point scale (clearly option 1 ... clearly option 2), plus sacred-value ratings per option, decision difficulty and negative emotions.
other_sources.human_data: Means and SDs only; decision responses not analysed per item. No per-item choice proportions; no raw-data repository found.

article.licence: CC BY 3.0 per Cambridge Core; conflicting with the journal's own statement that its 2013 CC BY switch was not retroactive
article.quote_verbatim: The authors license this article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 License.

quote_verbatim: As of March 2013, these articles are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 License (cc-by).
It is not retroactive to articles published earlier, so the original copyright statement still applies to them.
The copyright of contributions remains with the authors, except that it is assumed that authors consent to the following:

journal_policy.note: journal.sjdm.org redirects to jbaron.org. When and how the 2008 article was relicensed for Cambridge Core is not verified.

other_sources.verdict_note: Structurally a fit, but the licence evidence conflicts. Not adapted now (time-boxed): no stimulus text is copied; reuse only after the relicensing is confirmed or the authors agree, with attribution. No human choice shares to show.
other_sources.values_covered: Sacred (protected) values vs secular values: human safety and environmental protection vs profit, salary or vacation; taboo, tragic and routine trade-offs.
other_sources.paired_priority_suitability: Two options per scenario, and a priority sentence for each side maps naturally. Limits: about 10 overlapping scenarios, abbreviated translations, no per-item human choice benchmark, and taboo trade-offs may trigger model refusals unrelated to the priority.

other_sources.citation: Ponizovskiy, V., Grigoryan, L., Kühnen, U., & Boehnke, K. (2019). Social construction of the value-behavior relation. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 934.
other_sources.identity_check: Verified as the paper with value vignettes (PMC6504687). Not the Ponizovskiy et al. (2020) European Journal of Personality paper (Personal Values Dictionary, doi 10.1002/per.2294), which has no vignettes.

where: Appendix A in the supplementary material: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00934/full#supplementary-material
PMC copies Data_Sheet_1.docx / Data_Sheet_2.docx: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6504687/ (which file holds Appendix A not verified; files not opened)

other_sources.original_task: Online experiment (MTurk, N = 1,724 analysed): three trials, each one vignette describing a single behaviour (e.g. hiring, sharing a ride, enrolling in a course) framed as instantiating a value positively, negatively, or neutrally; attitude and intention ratings on 7-point scales; values measured separately with a questionnaire.
other_sources.human_data: Moderation analyses only; no per-item choice proportions. Raw-data availability not verified.

article.quote_verbatim: This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). The use, distribution or reproduction in other forums is permitted, provided the original author(s) and the copyright owner(s) are credited and that the original publication in this journal is cited, in accordance with accepted academic practice.

supplementary.quote_verbatim: All Frontiers articles are published with open access under the CC-BY Creative Commons attribution license.
supplementary.note: The policy does not mention supplementary files; the supplementary .docx files were not opened, so their own terms are unchecked.

other_sources.verdict_note: Not a two-option choice: each vignette describes one behaviour that is rated. Using it would mean writing new trade-off content, so it cannot supply published two-option stimuli. Cite for the value-instantiation idea. (At most adaptable as a loose template.)
other_sources.values_covered: Schwartz 19-value model: universalism-concern, security-personal, conformity-rules (one per trial).
other_sources.paired_priority_suitability: Poor as written: one behaviour per vignette, no second option, no per-item choice data.

other_sources.citation: Feather, N. T. (1995). Values, valences, and choice: The influence of values on the perceived attractiveness and choice of alternatives. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 68(6), 1135-1151.

where: Only in the paywalled APA article; no supplement, open copy or repository found.

other_sources.original_task: University students (N = 239) completed a values survey and then 10 hypothetical scenarios, each with two alternative courses of action; they rated the attractiveness of each alternative and chose one. (High-level description only; no stimulus text reproduced.)
other_sources.human_data: None openly available; per-item choice proportions not checked (full text not accessed).

article.licence: not verified; assumed © American Psychological Association, all rights reserved (standard for JPSP)
article.note: PsycNet did not render (page showed only 'Loading…'); no copyright line could be quoted. Treated as all rights reserved.

other_sources.verdict_note: Conceptual precedent (values predict the attractiveness and choice of two alternatives). No reuse rights; no stimulus text is stored or shown.
other_sources.values_covered: Schwartz value types (openness to change vs conservation; self-enhancement vs self-transcendence).
other_sources.paired_priority_suitability: Structurally ideal (two alternatives per scenario) but no reusable text or rights.

items.title: Two concert seats, two prices

original.scenario: I buy concert tickets on the internet for my brother and myself. I can get two seats side by side. However, the tickets fall into two different price categories, so that one ticket is 10 € more expensive than the other. What do I do?
original.option_other_regarding: I take the more expensive ticket.
original.option_order_note: Listed as in S1 Table: altruistic first, egoistic second (a priori classes). Singer counterbalanced the order shown to participants.
original.source_ref: S1 Table (pone.0214747.s001.docx), table row 2 (0 = header; item number rendered by Word auto-numbering numId=2)

value_conflict.label: Other-regarding vs self-regarding (EMCS altruistic vs egoistic)

human.basis: S1 Table item difficulty: proportion of altruistic choices, Studies 1 and 3, available data from up to 150 participants
human.rating_basis: Study 2 (n=50), rating of the response from 1 = egoistic to 7 = altruistic
notes: difficulty: S1 Table 0.61 vs S2 Table 0.58 (unexplained in source; S1 states 'available data'; possibly different missing-data handling).

screening.reason: Who pays for which ticket (and whether the pricier seat is better) is implicit; 'other-interest' could favour either ticket. Option-to-beneficiary mapping ambiguous.
screening.coded_by: one coder (an AI agent) from the verbatim text; a second coder is recommended

items.eligibility_note: Not usable: which option serves other people is ambiguous.
